source_review.notes: Checked current RFC Editor publications for host communication requirements, IPv6, TCP, UDP, ICMPv6, IPv4 identification, fragmentation robustness and IPv4/IPv6 path-MTU discovery, plus current Linux networking-scaling documentation. All ten cited URLs returned HTTP 200 after normal redirects; normative protocol rules, Linux mechanisms, abstract models, operational guidance and assurance remain separately scoped.

evidence: Checked packet backing, cursor, extents, namespace, header chain, validation, fragments, route, hooks, endpoint state, queue and accounting notation.
Reviewed nested extents, parser budgets, fragment intervals, endpoint lookup, queue limits and validation-certificate preservation.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation separates accessible bytes, protocol-declared structure, bounded work, reassembly coverage, lookup context, lifetime and admission accounting.

evidence: Executed a 24-byte reassembly model with fragments [0,8), [16,24) and [8,16).
Confirmed missing-byte counts 16, 8 and 0, rejection logic for out-of-range or overlapping intervals and complete final coverage.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic computation validates one interval-coverage sequence only; it implements no IP parser, fragment queue, checksum, timer, hook, namespace, kernel or packet.

evidence: Re-derived subtraction-based cursor bounds and nesting of each inner protocol extent within its validated parent.
Checked complete fragment coverage, finite parser-budget descent, endpoint lifetime token and object-plus-byte queue bounds.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The relations are subsystem reasoning tools and do not claim a complete formalization of IPv4, IPv6, transport protocols, Linux networking or policy hooks.

evidence: Reviewed every truncation boundary, contradictory declared lengths, integer overflow, maximum option chains, unknown headers, nonlinear access and nesting limits.
Reviewed reordered, duplicate, gapped and overlapping fragments, timer races, hash collisions, checksum states, hook reinjection, queue pressure, endpoint close, CPU hotplug and namespace teardown.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Byte, grammar, work, fragment, checksum, policy, lookup, lifetime, queue, error and teardown boundaries receive distinct treatment.

evidence: Traced receive parsing, extension walking, checksum validation, reassembly, hooks, local or forwarding selection, protocol dispatch, endpoint lookup, admission and output.
Verified monotonic trust, bounded work, complete context, protected lookup lifetime, charged queue insertion, rate-limited control traffic and one ownership outcome.
invariant_checking.notes: The chapter treats packet bytes, cached metadata, fragments, namespaces, routes, hooks, endpoints, queues and errors as coupled but independently validated state.

evidence: Reviewed IPv4 and IPv6 extents, options and extensions, checksums, fragmentation, hooks, forwarding, transport demultiplexing, endpoint lookup and control errors.
Constructed counterexamples for received-length-as-structure, coverage-as-valid-reassembly, checksum-as-authentication, hash-match-as-live-endpoint and reinjection-as-arbitrary-jump.
proof_review.notes: The chapter supplies reusable protocol-processing obligations, not a formal proof of an RFC, Linux, a network namespace, hook, route, transport implementation or application.

evidence: Audited uses of accessible, declared, parsed, validated, checksummed, reassembled, accepted, routed, matched, queued, delivered and released.
Confirmed normative standards rules, Linux behavior, abstract models, recommendations, tests and assurance claims remain separately scoped.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Byte arrival is not labeled protocol validity, coverage is not labeled legal reassembly, checksum success is not labeled authorization and endpoint lookup is not labeled application delivery.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-074/report.json records source, expected and actual output, stderr, exit status, toolchain and environment for the bounded fragment-coverage model.
Reviewed required kernel, namespace, protocol, hook, route, offload, device, CPU, workload, fault, capture and observer evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing toy establishes one abstract interval sequence only; it provides no evidence for IP conformance, Linux parsing, reassembly safety, policy behavior, endpoint lifetime or performance.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed protocol processing as monotonic construction of bounded trust from untrusted bytes through header, checksum, fragment, policy, route, transport, endpoint and admission proofs.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed protocol mechanisms as implementable concerns, including cursor-safe parsing, metadata invalidation, bounded reassembly, hook continuations, RCU-aware lookup, queue accounting and ICMP suppression. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from byte extents and variable headers through checksums, fragments, hooks, forwarding, protocol and endpoint lookup, admission, errors, output, observability and testing, followed by twelve obligations, sixteen trade-offs, twenty-five misconceptions, ten examples and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external operating-systems academic, IETF, Linux networking, protocol-implementation, network-operator, security, performance, independent-verification or certification review is claimed.
